bib.title: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models", Neel Guha, Julian Nyarko, Daniel E. Ho, Christopher Ré, plus 36 more. No venue is printed; the PDF is stamped "arXiv:2308.11462v1 [cs.CL] 20 Aug 2023" and dated August 23, 2023, so cite it as a preprint. First-author affiliation as printed: Stanford University (the first four starred authors are all Stanford).

COVERAGE: 143 pages, about 512k characters.
- Read in full: pp. 1-19 (main body), 27-35 (acknowledgements, limitations, datasheet, licences, availability, reasoning-type tables), 41-47 (NLP-type table, size buckets, Appendix E evaluation, F.1 Abercrombie, F.2 Canada Tax Court), 120-125 (models, shot counts, rule-application, rule-recall, issue-spotting and commercial rule-conclusion results).
- Skimmed: pp. 20-26 (references, checked for origins only); pp. 36-40 (Table 13 per-task sizes, first rows only); pp. 48-119 (per-task appendix F.3-F.33), where I read the opening of every "Construction process" paragraph for all task families and the fuller construction text for pp. 48, 69, 73, 78, 93 and 104, but not the backgrounds or example tables; pp. 126-143 (per-task tables 69-79, headers and a few rows).

CLAIMS
- claim: The benchmark has 162 tasks from 36 corpora, assembled by the paper's authors.
  number: 162 tasks, 36 sources
  setup: v1, August 2023, English only
  quote: "came together to assemble 162 tasks (from 36 different data sources)"
  where: p. 4
- claim: Tasks come from three sources: reused public datasets (reformatted), unreleased datasets hand-coded by legal scholars, and tasks written for LegalBench.
  number: none
  setup: a call for tasks in August 2022; submissions "vetted for legal correctness and task validity"; contributors are the authors. The paper prints no contributor count; the byline lists 40 names (my count).
  quote: "The last category of tasks are those that were developed specifically for LEGAL BENCH , by the authors of this paper."
  where: pp. 9-10
- claim: The taxonomy has six reasoning types, four from IRAC plus two more.
  number: 6
  setup: IRAC is used only as a grouping principle; each task tests one type
  quote: "(1) issue-spotting, (2) rule-recall, (3) rule-application, (4) rule-conclusion, (5) interpretation, and (6) rhetorical-understanding"
  where: p. 6
- claim: The task mix is heavily skewed towards interpretation.
  number: 119 of 162
  setup: Section 4.2 counts; rule-application reuses the rule-conclusion tasks
  quote: "rule-recall (5 tasks), issue-spotting (16 tasks), rule-application (16 tasks), rule-conclusion (16 tasks), interpretation (119 tasks), and rhetorical-understanding (10 tasks)"
  where: p. 10
- claim: Tasks are small, and train splits are tiny by design.
  number: at least 50, mean 563; train splits of 2-8
  setup: Table 12 buckets: 50-100 (28 tasks), 100-500 (97), 500-2000 (29), 2000+ (8). Formats: 112 binary, 35 multiple choice, 8 multi-class, 7 open generation.
  quote: "All LEGAL BENCH tasks contain at least 50 samples, with an average task size of 563 samples"
  where: p. 10; p. 30 ("between 2-8 instances"); p. 42
- claim: Classification is graded by exact match and reported as balanced accuracy; multi-answer tasks use F1.
  number: none
  setup: extraction outputs normalised; sara_numeric counts within 10% as correct
  quote: "Because some tasks contain significant label imbalances, we use balanced-accuracy as a metric."
  where: p. 13; p. 43
- claim: Rule-application and rule_qa are graded by hand against a released answer guide, on two measures: correctness and analysis.
  number: 30 instances sampled per diversity task; other tasks graded in full
  setup: GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Claude-1 only; "a law-trained individual" (singular)
  quote: "Rule-application tasks were evaluated manually by a law-trained individual, who analyzed LLM responses for both correctness and analysis."
  where: p. 13, footnote 9
- claim: GPT-4 leads on category averages; rule-recall is the weakest category for every model.
  number: GPT-4 82.9 / 59.2 / 89.9 / 75.2 / 79.4 (issue, rule, conclusion, interpretation, rhetorical)
  setup: 20 models; 0-8 hand-picked demonstrations (Table 58 lists up to 9); temperature 0.0; same prompt for all models except Claude formatting
  quote: "GPT-4 82.9 59.2 89.9 75.2 79.4" / "GPT-3.5 60.9 46.3 78.0 72.6 66.7" / "Claude-1 58.1 57.7 79.5 67.4 68.9"
  where: Table 2, p. 14
- claim: On rule-application, getting the answer right and showing the reasoning diverge.
  number: correctness / analysis: GPT-4 82.2 / 79.7; GPT-3.5 58.5 / 44.2; Claude 61.4 / 59.0
  setup: manual grading, 12 tasks
  quote: "GPT-4 82.2 79.7" / "GPT-3.5 58.5 44.2"
  where: Table 3, p. 14
- claim: Scores are highly sensitive to which demonstrations are chosen.
  number: over 20 points
  setup: 8 binary tasks, 5 random 4-shot prompts each, GPT-3.5 and Incite-Instruct-7B; permutation test p < 0.01
  quote: "the best Incite-Instruct prompt improves upon the worst prompt by over 20 points (balanced-accuracy)"
  where: p. 20
- claim: Plain-language prompts beat legalese on four of five tasks.
  number: up to 21 points
  setup: GPT-3.5, five tasks; one task reversed
  quote: "the plain-language prompt significantly outperforms the technical language prompt, by up to 21 points (balanced-accuracy)"
  where: p. 19
- claim: Contamination is conceded, not measured; tasks are sorted by prior web availability instead.
  number: none
  setup: Table 9 has three buckets: previously published, original but available, original and unavailable. Two tasks use post-cutoff data (2023 circuit opinions for citation prediction; 2022-23 ethics digests).
  quote: "It is thus possible that some LEGAL BENCH tasks leaked into pretraining data."
  where: p. 12; p. 35; pp. 48, 93

LIMITS
- Stated: no long documents; only tasks with objectively correct answers; English only; skewed to US law and contracts; IRAC steps are tested separately, never chained; results are a "lower-bound" because prompts were not tuned; no model above 13B among the open-source set.
- Stated: 16 of 17 issue-spotting tasks come from one source (Learned Hands), which skews that average.
- Unstated: no human baseline; no inter-annotator agreement for the manual grading (one grader); no confidence intervals on Table 2; no contamination experiment. Slices are tiny (n = 12-29).
- Internal inconsistency: Section 4.2 says 16 issue-spotting, 16 application and 119 interpretation tasks; Section 4.3 says 17, 12 and 118.
- Two tasks used ChatGPT during construction (Canada Tax Court pre-labelling; NYS Judicial Ethics question rewriting).
- Dated: models are GPT-4, GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) and Claude-1 v1.3, queried May-August 2023.

BUILDS ON: IRAC via Stockmeyer (2021) [124] and Ellsworth, "Legal reasoning" [47]; collaborative model from BigBench (Srivastava et al.) [123]; HELM [80] for exact match and task organisation; RAFT (Alex et al., 2021) [1] for few-shot splits; CUAD [62], ContractNLI [74], MAUD [142], OPP-115 [149], SARA [65] as reused data; datasheets [55]; the authors' own 2022 call for tasks [59].

CODE: none.

FIGURES: Figure 3, p. 20: "We evaluate GPT-3.5 and Incite-Instruct on five prompts constructed by randomly selecting different samples to use as in-context demonstrations". It shows the spread per task at a glance, which is the prompt-sensitivity point. (Table 9, p. 35, is the better candidate for the contamination point, but it is a table.)

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean; "LEGAL BENCH" is split by small caps and Table 13 and the results tables are flattened into rows. No embedded instructions found. Working text is at /tmp/lb_txt/all.txt (page-marked); source is /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/guha-2023-legalbench.pdf.
